text: FMD (Foot-and-Mouth Disease) in swine is caused by a virus (antibiotics cannot treat it); of the 7 strains worldwide, 3 (O, A, Asia1) have been identified in Cambodia. Transmission: the virus is very resistant in the environment and can travel on the wind; the main route is respiratory aerosols (airborne droplets) from infected to healthy pigs; people can carry the virus on shoes, clothes, hands, and hair, and it can survive 1–2 days in the human respiratory tract, spreading further to animals. FMD in pigs is highly contagious and spreads fast but pigs only shed virus for a short time (not long-term carriers), so outbreaks usually run only a few weeks. Symptoms usually appear 3–5 days after contact: fever and vesicles (blisters) on the feet, mouth, and teats are the hallmark signs; severe hoof lesions on the coronary band and between the toes make pigs unable to walk or eat, causing intense pain and vocalizing; vesicles are also often seen on the snout. Treatment can only manage secondary infection and pain, not cure the disease: Paracetamol for inflammation/pain/fever; TMP+Sulfa or Tetracyclines against bacterial infection of the foot lesions; local treatment with a wound spray combining disinfectant (Methylene Blue or Gentian Violet) and Tetracycline, applied twice daily after washing lesions with soap; since sick pigs can't walk to feed/water, individual feeding and watering is important. Prevention: monovalent vaccine (strain O only, the most common strain in Cambodian pigs) or trivalent (O+A+Asia1); vaccination only works in pigs if given regularly, since pigs mount a weaker immune response than cattle do; recommended to vaccinate sows with trivalent vaccine twice a year, plus a booster during a provincial outbreak; piglets/growing pigs given the monovalent vaccine can still show FMD signs.
